text:
Detroit's season has one headline and it isn't on the scoresheet. Dylan Larkin told the Red Wings he would no longer play for them, and on October 29 they suspended him without pay. Since then it's been a trade watch: The Athletic's Michael Russo reported the Wild are pushing hard, the Bruins have been linked, and the latest reports have Larkin taking a hard line on where he'll go. Until something gives, the Red Wings are a team without their best center, playing to prove they can be fine anyway.

So far, the hockey says they can. Detroit is 7-7-3 but takes 52% of the expected goals (the quality of chances for and against), and has scored nine fewer goals than those chances usually produce. Our numbers figure they've left about two and a half points on the table. The kids are the bright side: Alex DeBrincat with Emmitt Finnie and Michael Brandsegg-Nygard has outscored opponents 8-1 at five on five with 64% of the chances, and Viktor Arvidsson, signed as a free agent, has been the story that headline writers reached for instead, hat trick and all.

The worry is in net. John Gibson has been well below what his shots deserve after a strong season last year, and Ben Chiarot and Moritz Seider have been outscored 9-5 together at an even split of chances.

Playoff odds of 32% are the price of a slow start, not proof of a bad team. The bigger number is whatever Detroit gets back for Larkin. A deal that lands a top center changes this season; one that doesn't makes the finishing luck turning the only way up.
headline: The Larkin standoff, and the team playing through it
